title: AI Unlocked: Law & Legal Practice
blurb: For lawyers, paralegals, and compliance teams: research and drafting acceleration, contract review workflows, the legal-AI tool market compared, and the professional-responsibility rules (competence, confidentiality, candor) that make or break adoption.

modules.d: What AI changes in legal work, the duties that do not change, and the cautionary cases every lawyer must know.
modules.body:
Law is a language profession — and AI is a language technology

Much legal work is reading, analysing and producing text: research memos, contracts, pleadings, opinions, correspondence. Generative AI therefore touches the core of legal practice more directly than most professions. Used well, it compresses hours of first-draft work and document review into minutes. Used carelessly, it produces confident, polished, entirely fictional law.

The cautionary case

In Mata v. Avianca (U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York, 2023), lawyers filed a brief citing judicial decisions that did not exist — generated by ChatGPT. When questioned, they did not promptly correct the record. The court imposed sanctions, finding they had abandoned their responsibilities. Since then, courts in many jurisdictions have reported similar incidents of fabricated citations and misquoted authorities, with sanctions, costs orders and disciplinary referrals. The lesson is not "never use AI"; it is every authority must be verified in an authoritative source by a lawyer before it is relied on.

Specialised tools are not immune. A 2024 Stanford study of leading AI legal research tools from major legal publishers found that even systems grounded in legal databases produced incorrect or misgrounded answers in a meaningful share of test queries. Better tools reduce the risk; they do not remove the duty to verify.

Professional duties that do not change

Codes of professional conduct differ across jurisdictions, but core duties are remarkably consistent:

  • Competence — including understanding the benefits and risks of the technology you use. The American Bar Association's Model Rules (comment 8 to Rule 1.1) explicitly include technological competence, and ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024) applies the Model Rules to generative AI.
  • Confidentiality — protecting client information, including from tools that store or train on inputs.
  • Candour to the tribunal — never presenting false statements of law or fact; correcting errors promptly.
  • Supervision — responsibility for the work of juniors, staff and the tools they use.
  • Communication — keeping clients informed, including about significant use of AI where relevant.
  • Reasonable fees — billing that reflects the work actually done.
  • Independence and judgement — the lawyer, not the tool, provides legal advice.

Practising in a mixed legal system

Many African jurisdictions combine legal traditions, and AI tools trained mainly on US and UK material handle them poorly. Cameroon is bijural: common-law traditions apply in the North-West and South-West regions and civil-law traditions elsewhere, with statutes in English and French, alongside customary law. Business law is largely harmonised through the OHADA Uniform Acts, interpreted by national courts and the Common Court of Justice and Arbitration (CCJA) in Abidjan. An AI tool may confidently apply English common law or French civil law to a question governed by an OHADA Uniform Act or Cameroonian statute. Jurisdiction-specific verification is therefore essential.

Where AI adds value in legal work

  • Summarising long documents, judgments, transcripts and contracts.
  • First drafts of standard documents, letters and clauses from approved templates.
  • Issue spotting and structuring research questions.
  • Comparing documents and identifying deviations from a standard.
  • Translation between English and French — with legal review of terms of art.
  • Plain-language explanations for clients.
  • Large-scale document review in disputes and due diligence, with appropriate validation.

The changing shape of legal work

As routine drafting and review accelerate, value shifts toward judgement, strategy, negotiation, advocacy, client relationships and verification. Junior lawyers still need to learn the fundamentals — otherwise they cannot evaluate AI output. Firms and legal departments must redesign training so juniors learn with AI without skipping the skills that make them competent.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal practice AI advisor. Ask me about my jurisdiction(s), practice area, firm or department size and current tools. Identify five use cases where AI could save the most time with manageable risk, and for each specify the verification step and confidentiality safeguard required. Then list the professional-conduct duties in my jurisdiction that I should check apply to AI use, noting that I must verify them against the official rules.

📚 Glossary

  • Fabricated citation: an AI-generated reference to a case or authority that does not exist
  • Technological competence: understanding the benefits and risks of the technology a lawyer uses
  • Candour to the tribunal: duty not to mislead the court on law or fact
  • Bijural system: a legal system combining two legal traditions
  • OHADA: Organisation for the Harmonisation of Business Law in Africa

📖 References

  • Mata v. Avianca, Inc., No. 22-cv-1461 (S.D.N.Y. 2023) — sanctions order.
  • American Bar Association — Model Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.1 cmt. 8; Formal Opinion 512 (2024) on generative AI tools.
  • Magesh, V. et al. (2024). Hallucination-free? Assessing the reliability of leading AI legal research tools. Stanford RegLab/HAI.
  • OHADA — Treaty and Uniform Acts; Common Court of Justice and Arbitration (CCJA).

quiz.q: A junior lawyer uses an AI tool to find supporting cases for a brief. The tool returns six well-formatted citations. What MUST happen before filing?
opts: Retrieve and read each authority in an authoritative source to confirm it exists and supports the proposition
Use only the cases the tool rated most relevant
Ask the AI tool to confirm the cases are real
Check that the citations are correctly formatted
quiz.x: After Mata v. Avianca and similar cases, every authority must be verified in an authoritative source by a lawyer. Asking the AI to confirm itself is not verification.

quiz.q: After filing, a lawyer discovers that one cited case does not exist. What does the duty of candour require?
opts: Wait to see whether opposing counsel notices
Promptly correct the record with the court
Quietly remove the case in the next filing
quiz.x: Candour requires prompt correction of false statements of law; delay aggravated the sanctions in Mata.

quiz.q: A firm adopts a specialised legal research AI built on a major legal database. Which statement is MOST accurate?
opts: Only junior lawyers need to verify outputs
The risk of errors is reduced but not eliminated, so verification remains required
quiz.x: Research found even specialised tools produced incorrect or misgrounded answers in some queries.

quiz.q: An AI tool answers a question about a commercial company's capital requirements in Cameroon by citing French company law. What is the MOST likely error?
opts: The tool should have cited English common law
The question is governed by the OHADA Uniform Act on commercial companies, which the tool did not apply
None, since French law applies in Cameroon
quiz.x: OHADA Uniform Acts govern company law in member states; tools trained on other systems may misapply law.

quiz.q: Which duty MOST directly requires lawyers to understand how AI tools work and fail?
quiz.x: Competence includes understanding the benefits and risks of technology used.

quiz.q: Which task is the STRONGEST candidate for AI assistance with appropriate review?
opts: Advising a client without lawyer review
Summarising a 200-page deposition transcript for the supervising lawyer
quiz.x: Summarising is time-consuming and reviewable; strategy, opinions and advice require lawyer judgement.

quiz.q: A partner says juniors no longer need to learn legal research because AI does it. What is the MAIN risk?
opts: Juniors will be unable to evaluate whether AI output is correct
AI tools will become more expensive
quiz.x: Without fundamental skills, lawyers cannot detect AI errors.

quiz.q: A supervising partner did not review a junior's AI-assisted memo that contained errors. Which duty is MOST implicated?
quiz.x: Supervisors are responsible for the work of juniors and the tools they use.

quiz.q: Why is translation between English and French a particularly sensitive AI use in Cameroonian practice?
opts: Legal terms of art differ between common-law and civil-law traditions and may be mistranslated
quiz.x: Terms such as 'consideration' or 'cause' carry system-specific legal meanings requiring legal review.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST captures the lesson of the fabricated-citation cases?
opts: AI may assist, but lawyers remain responsible for verifying every authority they rely on
Only senior lawyers may use AI
quiz.x: Responsibility and verification, not prohibition, are the lesson.

modules.d: Structured, verifiable workflows for legal research, analysis and drafting.
modules.body:
Research: AI as accelerator, not authority

A disciplined AI-assisted research workflow keeps authoritative sources at the centre. Step 1 — Frame the question: identify the jurisdiction, governing law, facts, procedural posture and the precise legal question. AI can help break a complex problem into sub-issues and suggest search terms in English and French. Step 2 — Find the law in authoritative sources: official gazettes, codes, OHADA Uniform Acts, court reporters, recognised databases. AI-integrated research platforms can speed this, but the source documents are what count. Step 3 — Read and analyse the actual texts. AI can summarise long judgments and extract holdings, but you must read the relevant passages yourself. Step 4 — Synthesise the rule and its application. Step 5 — Verify every citation, quotation, pinpoint reference and the current status of the law (amended, repealed, overruled, appealed).

Quotation discipline. AI tools frequently "quote" language that does not appear in the source, or blend paraphrase and quotation. Never put text in quotation marks unless you have copied it from the authoritative source yourself and checked the page or paragraph reference.

Structuring analysis: IRAC and its variants

Legal analysis is commonly structured as Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion (IRAC), or CREAC (Conclusion, Rule, Explanation, Application, Conclusion) for persuasive writing. In civil-law traditions, the syllogisme juridique — major premise (rule), minor premise (facts), conclusion — serves the same purpose. AI is helpful for testing structure: ask it to identify which element is weak, which counter-arguments are unaddressed, and which facts are missing.

Drafting with templates and playbooks

The most reliable drafting workflows begin from approved precedents — the firm's or department's templates and clause library — rather than AI generating documents from nothing. Provide AI with the template, the deal terms or facts, and specific instructions; ask it to adapt clauses, flag deviations and draft explanatory notes. This keeps drafts consistent with house standards and reduces the risk of invented or foreign-law clauses.

Drafting principles AI should follow — and you should check

  • Precision: defined terms used consistently; obligations clear ("shall" or "must" for obligations, "may" for discretions).
  • Completeness: the document addresses the events that matter — termination, breach, disputes, notices, governing law and jurisdiction.
  • Coherence: no conflicting clauses or broken cross-references after edits.
  • Plain language where possible, especially for consumer and employment documents.
  • Jurisdictional fit: governing law, mandatory local rules (e.g., OHADA provisions, local consumer or labour protections) and enforceability.

Litigation drafting

Pleadings, submissions and correspondence carry the highest risk because they go to courts and opponents. Use AI for outlines, organising facts chronologically, drafting non-authoritative sections and checking consistency between facts and exhibits. Every authority, factual assertion and quotation must be verified. Some courts now require disclosure or certification regarding AI use in filings; check the rules and practice directions of the relevant court.

Client communication

AI is excellent at converting complex advice into clear explanations for clients — summaries, options with pros and cons, next steps. Ensure simplification does not change the legal meaning, and that the advice remains the lawyer's.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal research and drafting assistant. Step 1: help me frame a research question by jurisdiction, governing law, facts and sub-issues, with search terms in English and French. Step 2: when I paste authoritative extracts, help me structure an IRAC or syllogisme juridique analysis and identify weak points and counter-arguments. Step 3: adapt my approved template to the facts I give, flagging deviations and broken cross-references. Never invent authorities or quotations — mark any needed authority as [VERIFY].

📚 Glossary

  • IRAC / CREAC: structures for legal analysis and persuasive writing
  • Syllogisme juridique: civil-law reasoning from rule (major premise) to facts (minor premise) to conclusion
  • Pinpoint citation: reference to the exact page or paragraph
  • Precedent (drafting): an approved template document
  • Clause library: collection of approved standard clauses

📖 References

  • OHADA — Uniform Acts (official texts, ohada.org).
  • Garner, B. Legal Writing in Plain English.
  • Court practice directions on AI use — check the relevant jurisdiction.
  • Juricaf and AfricanLII — case-law databases (verify coverage).

quiz.q: An AI-generated memo includes a sentence in quotation marks attributed to a CCJA judgment. What should the lawyer do?
opts: Ask the AI for the paragraph number
Convert it to a paraphrase without checking
Keep it, since quotation marks indicate accuracy
Locate the judgment and confirm the exact wording and paragraph before quoting
quiz.x: AI often fabricates or blends quotations; only verified source text may be quoted.

quiz.q: What is the FIRST step in a disciplined AI-assisted research workflow?
opts: Frame the question: jurisdiction, governing law, facts, procedural posture and precise issue
quiz.x: Precise framing determines which law applies and what to search for.

quiz.q: A lawyer finds a statute provision supporting the client's case. Before relying on it, what must also be checked?
opts: Its current status — whether amended, repealed or affected by later law or decisions
quiz.x: Law changes; currency of the authority must be verified.

quiz.q: Which drafting approach is MOST reliable?
opts: Ask AI to draft a full share purchase agreement from scratch
Start from the firm's approved precedent and use AI to adapt it to the deal terms, flagging deviations
Copy a contract from a foreign website
quiz.x: Approved precedents keep drafts consistent with house standards and applicable law.

quiz.q: After AI edits, clause 14.2 refers to 'clause 9.4', which no longer exists. Which drafting principle is affected?
quiz.x: Edits frequently break cross-references; coherence checks are essential.

quiz.q: In civil-law reasoning, what does the 'minor premise' of the syllogisme juridique contain?
quiz.x: Major premise is the rule, minor premise the facts, then the conclusion.

quiz.q: A court's practice direction requires parties to disclose AI use in drafting submissions. A firm used AI for an outline. What should it do?
opts: Comply with the disclosure requirement as specified by the court
Ignore the rule since a lawyer revised the text
Ask the client whether to disclose
Rewrite the submission manually to avoid disclosure
quiz.x: Court rules must be followed; check practice directions in each forum.

quiz.q: Which use of AI in litigation is LOWEST risk?
opts: Generating authorities for the legal argument
Organising the facts and exhibits chronologically for the lawyer's review
Writing the final submission without review
quiz.x: Organising facts for review is helpful and verifiable; authorities and strategy require lawyer judgement and verification.

quiz.q: An AI-simplified client letter states the client 'can' terminate the contract at any time, while the advice was that termination is possible only for material breach. What is the problem?
opts: The client may not read it
quiz.x: Plain language must not alter the substance of advice.

quiz.q: Which practice MOST improves the quality of AI-assisted analysis?
opts: Asking AI for the final answer only
Asking AI to identify weak elements, unaddressed counter-arguments and missing facts in your analysis
quiz.x: Using AI as a critic strengthens the lawyer's own analysis.

modules.t: Tool Study: The Legal AI Market
modules.d: Evaluating legal AI by accuracy, grounding, confidentiality and jurisdictional coverage.
modules.body:
A rapidly evolving market

Legal technology now includes general AI assistants, AI features inside established research databases, contract analysis platforms, e-discovery systems and practice-management tools. Products and features change quickly; evaluate by criteria and verify current capabilities, coverage and terms directly with providers.

Main categories

  • General AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot): drafting, summarising, translation, analysis of documents you provide. Not legal research databases; may fabricate authorities if asked for law without sources.
  • AI-enabled legal research platforms from established publishers (for example Thomson Reuters' Westlaw and CoCounsel, LexisNexis' Lexis+ AI): answers grounded in their databases with links to sources. Coverage of African, OHADA and Cameroonian law may be limited — check.
  • Free and regional legal information sources: OHADA official texts, Juricaf (francophone supreme court case law), AfricanLII and national legal information institutes, official gazettes. AI tools may not index these; lawyers must search them directly.
  • Contract analysis and lifecycle management: extracting clauses, comparing against playbooks, tracking obligations and renewals.
  • E-discovery and document review: technology-assisted review (TAR) and AI classification for large document sets, with statistical validation.
  • Practice management: time recording, billing, matter management and knowledge management with AI features.
Grounding is the key technical question. A tool that retrieves relevant documents from a trusted database and generates answers linked to those documents (often called retrieval-augmented generation) is generally more reliable than one answering from its training alone. But grounding can still fail — wrong document retrieved, misread holding, outdated law. Links make verification faster; they do not replace it.

Evaluation criteria

  1. Accuracy: test with real questions from your practice where you know the correct answer.
  2. Grounding and citations: does every answer link to sources you can open and check?
  3. Jurisdictional coverage: does it include your jurisdictions, languages, OHADA texts and recent decisions?
  4. Confidentiality and security: is client data used for training, where is it stored, what certifications and contractual protections exist, can you control retention?
  5. Privilege protection: do terms and architecture preserve confidentiality sufficient to avoid privilege concerns?
  6. Integration: with document management, email and practice systems.
  7. Auditability: are queries and outputs logged for supervision?
  8. Cost and value: licence cost relative to time saved and quality gained.

Testing a legal AI tool properly

Build a test set of 20–30 questions from your practice with known answers, including tricky ones: recently changed law, jurisdiction-specific questions, questions where the law is unsettled, and questions mixing OHADA and national law. Score each tool on correctness, citation accuracy, honesty about uncertainty and usefulness. A tool that admits uncertainty is safer than one that answers everything confidently.

Firm and department strategy

Many practices start with an approved general assistant under a business agreement for drafting and summarising client-provided documents, plus their existing research databases for authorities. Specialised platforms follow where volume and coverage justify them. Establish an approved tools list and prohibit unapproved tools for client work.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal technology evaluator. Help me build a test set of 25 questions from my practice area and jurisdictions, including recently changed law, OHADA versus national law questions, and unsettled issues. Then design a scoring rubric covering correctness, citation accuracy, honesty about uncertainty and usefulness, and a list of confidentiality and privilege questions to ask each vendor.

📚 Glossary

  • Grounding: basing AI answers on retrieved source documents
  • Retrieval-augmented generation: AI that retrieves relevant documents before generating an answer
  • TAR: technology-assisted review in document-heavy matters
  • Juricaf: database of francophone supreme court case law
  • Approved tools list: the tools permitted for client work

📖 References

  • Magesh, V. et al. (2024). Reliability of AI legal research tools. Stanford RegLab/HAI.
  • Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe (S.D.N.Y. 2012) — early judicial approval of TAR.
  • OHADA (ohada.org), Juricaf, AfricanLII — legal information sources.
  • Vendor documentation — verify current coverage and terms.

quiz.q: A general AI assistant gives a detailed answer on OHADA arbitration law without citing any sources. What is the BEST response?
opts: Rely on it since it is detailed
Treat it as a starting point and find and verify the relevant OHADA Uniform Act and CCJA rules directly
Ask the same assistant for sources and accept them
Discard it and never use AI
quiz.x: General assistants are not authoritative research databases; verify with official sources.

quiz.q: Which feature MOST improves the verifiability of a legal AI tool's answers?
opts: Answers grounded in retrieved sources with links to the documents
quiz.x: Linked sources make verification efficient, though still required.

quiz.q: A major US legal research AI is excellent on US law. A Douala firm considers it for OHADA work. What is the KEY evaluation question?
opts: Is it popular in the US?
Does its database cover OHADA Uniform Acts, CCJA decisions and Cameroonian law in French and English?
Does it have a mobile app?
quiz.x: Jurisdictional coverage determines usefulness.

quiz.q: When testing legal AI tools, why include questions about recently changed law?
opts: Because tools may rely on outdated sources, and such questions reveal currency problems
quiz.x: Currency errors are common and dangerous.

quiz.q: Which tool behaviour is SAFER for legal research?
opts: Always giving a confident, complete answer
Acknowledging uncertainty or missing coverage when appropriate
quiz.x: Honesty about uncertainty reduces the risk of relying on false confidence.

quiz.q: A firm's lawyers use a variety of free AI tools for client documents. What should the firm establish FIRST?
opts: An approved tools list with confidentiality requirements and prohibition of unapproved tools for client work
quiz.x: Approved tools with appropriate protections are fundamental to confidentiality.

quiz.q: In large-scale document review for litigation, what makes technology-assisted review defensible?
opts: Transparent process with statistical validation of results
Reviewing only documents the AI selects without checks
quiz.x: Courts have accepted TAR where process and validation are sound.

quiz.q: Which vendor answer raises the GREATEST confidentiality concern?
opts: Inputs may be used to improve our models
Client data is stored in an encrypted environment and not used for training
quiz.x: Using client inputs for training risks confidentiality and privilege.

quiz.q: Why must lawyers still search sources such as Juricaf or official gazettes directly?
opts: They are the only legal sources
AI tools may not index regional and national sources, so relevant law may be missed
quiz.x: Coverage gaps mean AI-only research may be incomplete for African jurisdictions.

quiz.q: What is the BEST measure of a legal AI tool's value?
opts: Time saved and quality gained in real matters, relative to cost and risk
quiz.x: Value is measured in practice outcomes, balanced against cost and risk.

modules.d: Contract review playbooks, obligation tracking and regulatory compliance mapping with AI.
modules.body:
Contracts are data

Organisations hold thousands of contracts containing obligations, rights, deadlines and risks. Most are never systematically reviewed after signature — until something goes wrong. AI makes it practical to extract, compare and monitor contract terms at scale, turning static documents into manageable data.

The contract lifecycle

Request and drafting → negotiation and review → approval and signature → obligation management → renewal, amendment or termination. AI can assist at each stage: drafting from templates, comparing counterparty drafts against standards, summarising changes for approvers, extracting key dates and obligations into a register, and alerting before renewals and deadlines.

The review playbook

A contract review playbook records the organisation's positions on key clauses: preferred position, acceptable fallbacks, and unacceptable terms requiring escalation. Typical clauses: limitation of liability, indemnities, warranties, payment terms, intellectual property, confidentiality, data protection, termination, governing law and dispute resolution, and force majeure. With a playbook, AI can compare a counterparty draft clause by clause, classify each as standard, acceptable fallback or escalation, and propose redlines. Without a playbook, AI applies generic assumptions that may not reflect your risk appetite or your law.

Example. Playbook: "Limitation of liability — preferred: capped at 12 months' fees; fallback: capped at 2× annual fees; escalate: uncapped liability or exclusion of liability for our own data breaches." AI review: "Clause 11 caps supplier liability at fees paid in the previous 3 months — below fallback; propose 12 months and flag for negotiation." The lawyer confirms the reading and decides strategy.

Due diligence

In mergers, acquisitions and financings, AI can review large data rooms to identify change-of-control clauses, assignment restrictions, exclusivity, unusual indemnities and termination rights. Validate with sampling: lawyers review a statistically meaningful sample and all high-risk flags; the cost of a missed change-of-control clause can be severe.

Obligation management

Extracting obligations — delivery deadlines, reporting duties, service levels, notice periods, renewal dates — into a register with owners and alerts prevents missed deadlines, automatic renewals of unwanted contracts and breaches. AI extraction should be checked for key contracts; even small extraction errors on dates can have significant consequences.

Regulatory compliance mapping

Compliance teams must translate laws and regulations into internal obligations, controls and evidence. AI can help: summarising new regulations, mapping requirements to existing policies and controls, identifying gaps, and drafting control descriptions. For example, mapping data protection obligations — lawful basis, notices, data subject rights, security, breach notification, cross-border transfers — to the organisation's processes. As always, the authoritative regulatory text governs, and interpretation of ambiguous provisions requires legal judgement.

OHADA and cross-border contracts

Many contracts in Central and West Africa involve OHADA law, other national laws and international parties. Key considerations include choice of governing law, enforceability of arbitration clauses (OHADA Uniform Act on Arbitration; CCJA arbitration), language versions and which prevails, mandatory local rules, and currency and payment provisions. AI can help identify and compare these clauses across a portfolio; lawyers must assess enforceability.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my contract review assistant. First, help me build a review playbook for one contract type with preferred, fallback and escalation positions for the ten key clauses in this module, adapted to my governing law. Then, when I paste a counterparty draft (anonymised), compare it clause by clause, classify each as standard, fallback or escalation, propose redlines, and extract all dates and obligations into a register table. Mark any point needing lawyer judgement.

📚 Glossary

  • Review playbook: organisation's preferred, fallback and escalation positions on clauses
  • Change of control: clause triggered when ownership of a party changes
  • Obligation register: tracked list of contractual duties, deadlines and owners
  • Compliance mapping: linking legal requirements to internal controls and evidence
  • CCJA arbitration: arbitration administered under the OHADA Common Court of Justice and Arbitration

📖 References

  • World Commerce & Contracting — contract management resources.
  • OHADA — Uniform Act on Arbitration; CCJA Arbitration Rules.
  • OHADA — Uniform Act on General Commercial Law.
  • ICC — model contracts and arbitration rules.

quiz.q: An organisation uses AI to review supplier contracts without any playbook. What is the MAIN weakness?
opts: The AI applies generic assumptions that may not reflect the organisation's risk appetite or applicable law
quiz.x: A playbook encodes positions and escalation rules specific to the organisation.

quiz.q: Playbook fallback for liability cap is 2× annual fees. A draft caps liability at 6 months' fees. How should AI-assisted review classify it?
opts: Escalation or negotiation required — below the fallback
quiz.x: Six months' fees is below the acceptable fallback, so it requires negotiation or escalation.

quiz.q: In an acquisition data room of 3,000 contracts, AI flags 40 change-of-control clauses. What is the BEST validation approach?
opts: Ask the AI to double-check itself
Review all flagged contracts and a statistically meaningful sample of unflagged ones
quiz.x: Sampling unflagged contracts tests for missed clauses; flagged high-risk items need full review.

quiz.q: A software contract auto-renewed for three years because the notice deadline was missed. Which practice would MOST likely have prevented this?
opts: An obligation register with renewal dates, owners and alerts
quiz.x: Tracking dates and owners prevents missed notice periods.

quiz.q: AI extracts a renewal notice period of '90 days' from a key contract. The contract actually says '9 days'. What lesson does this illustrate?
opts: Key extracted data, especially dates, should be checked on important contracts
Contracts should not include notice periods
quiz.x: Small extraction errors on dates can have major consequences.

quiz.q: A compliance officer asks AI to map a new data protection regulation to company controls. What remains the lawyer's responsibility?
opts: Interpreting ambiguous provisions and confirming obligations against the authoritative text
quiz.x: AI can map and summarise; interpretation and confirmation require legal judgement.

quiz.q: A contract between a Cameroonian company and a French supplier has English and French versions that differ. Which clause is MOST important?
opts: A clause specifying which language version prevails
quiz.x: A prevailing-language clause resolves conflicts between versions.

quiz.q: Which clause type is MOST critical to check for enforceability in a cross-border OHADA contract?
quiz.x: Enforceability of dispute resolution determines whether rights can be enforced.

quiz.q: Which stage of the contract lifecycle is MOST often neglected in organisations?
quiz.x: After signature, contracts are often filed and forgotten until problems arise.

quiz.q: How should a lawyer treat AI-proposed redlines?
opts: Review them, confirm the reading of the clause and decide negotiation strategy
Send them unread to the counterparty
quiz.x: AI proposes; the lawyer decides.

modules.d: Protecting client confidences, privilege and professional integrity when using AI.
modules.body:
Confidentiality is the first question

Lawyers owe clients duties of confidentiality that are among the strongest in professional life. Entering client information into an AI tool is a disclosure to a third party's system. Whether that is acceptable depends on the tool's terms, security and data use, the sensitivity of the information, applicable professional rules and, where needed, the client's informed consent.

Key questions before using any AI tool with client information: Does the provider use inputs to train models? Who at the provider can access data, and where is it stored? How long is it retained, and can you delete it? Is there a contract with confidentiality and data protection obligations? Does it meet security standards? ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024), for example, advises that lawyers must evaluate these risks and, for some tools — especially those that may disclose information to others or learn from it — obtain clients' informed consent before inputting confidential information. Your own jurisdiction's rules should be checked.

Practical rule for practices. Client-confidential and privileged information goes only into approved tools under business or enterprise agreements with appropriate confidentiality, security and no-training terms. Consumer versions of AI tools, personal accounts and unapproved apps are prohibited for client work. When in doubt, anonymise or do not use the tool.

Legal privilege

Legal professional privilege (or the attorney–client privilege and work-product protection in some systems, or secret professionnel in civil-law traditions) protects certain communications and materials from disclosure. Privilege can be lost through disclosure to third parties outside the protected relationship. Whether using an AI provider waives privilege depends on jurisdiction, the tool's confidentiality arrangements and how it is used. Reduce risk by using tools under strict confidentiality terms, limiting what is shared, and following firm policy.

Supervision and responsibility

Partners and supervising lawyers remain responsible for work produced by juniors, paralegals and non-lawyer staff, including their use of AI. Practices should establish policies, training, approved tools and review procedures. "The AI did it" is not a defence in disciplinary proceedings or before a court.

Fees and billing

If AI reduces the time taken, hourly billing must reflect time actually spent. Charging clients for hours saved by AI, or for the lawyer's time learning a general tool, is generally inappropriate. Practices may consider value-based or fixed fees that reflect the value delivered. Costs of AI tools may be charged only where permitted and agreed. Transparency with clients about billing arrangements protects trust.

Candour, fairness and the court

Lawyers must not mislead courts on law or fact, must correct errors promptly, and must comply with any court rules on AI disclosure. They must also deal fairly with opponents — for example, not using AI to fabricate evidence or alter documents. Deepfake audio, video and images present new evidentiary challenges; lawyers should be alert to the possibility that evidence has been manipulated and seek authentication where appropriate.

Communication with clients

Clients should be informed about significant uses of AI that affect their matter, especially where confidential information is involved, where it affects fees, or where clients have expressed preferences. Many corporate clients now issue outside-counsel guidelines specifying AI use requirements; follow them.

Bias and access to justice

AI can widen access to legal information for people who cannot afford lawyers — but it can also provide confident wrong advice to those least able to detect it, and reproduce biases in legal data. Lawyers and legal organisations deploying public-facing legal AI should design for accuracy, clear limitations, escalation to human help and fairness.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal ethics advisor. I will describe how I plan to use an AI tool on a client matter. Analyse the confidentiality, privilege, supervision, fee and candour implications, list the questions I must answer about the tool's terms, state whether client informed consent may be needed, and draft a short client communication explaining our AI use. Remind me to verify the rules of my own bar or law society.

📚 Glossary

  • Legal professional privilege: protection of certain lawyer–client communications from disclosure
  • Secret professionnel: civil-law professional secrecy obligation
  • Informed consent: client agreement after explanation of risks and alternatives
  • Outside-counsel guidelines: client rules for external lawyers, increasingly including AI
  • Deepfake: AI-manipulated audio, video or image

📖 References

  • American Bar Association — Formal Opinion 512 (2024), Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools.
  • Law Society of England and Wales — Generative AI: the essentials.
  • Bar associations and law societies — check your jurisdiction's AI guidance.
  • Barreau du Cameroun — rules of professional conduct (verify current texts).

quiz.q: A lawyer pastes a client's confidential merger documents into a personal, free AI account to summarise them. What is the MAIN problem?
opts: Confidential information is disclosed to a tool without approved confidentiality, security and data-use terms
The client may prefer a different format
The summary may be too short
quiz.x: Client information may only go into approved tools with appropriate protections.

quiz.q: Which vendor term MOST threatens confidentiality and potentially privilege?
opts: Inputs used to train models available to other users
quiz.x: Training use may expose client information beyond the protected relationship.

quiz.q: An AI tool reduces a research task from 10 hours to 2 hours. How should an hourly-billing lawyer bill?
opts: The time actually spent, about 2 hours, unless a different fee arrangement was agreed
Nothing, since AI did the work
quiz.x: Hourly billing reflects actual time; value-based arrangements must be agreed transparently.

quiz.q: A paralegal used an unapproved AI tool, causing errors in a filing. Who bears professional responsibility?
opts: The supervising lawyer, who remains responsible for supervised work
Nobody, since it was an accident
quiz.x: Supervisors are responsible for supervised work and must establish policies and review.

quiz.q: A corporate client's outside-counsel guidelines prohibit using generative AI on its matters without approval. What should the firm do?
opts: Use AI only for internal notes
Comply with the guidelines and seek approval before any use
Use AI anyway if it improves quality
Ignore the guidelines for small tasks
quiz.x: Client instructions govern use on their matters.

quiz.q: Opposing party submits an audio recording that sounds like the client making admissions. The client says it is fake. What is the MOST appropriate step?
opts: Consider seeking forensic authentication of the recording
Ask AI whether it is real
quiz.x: Deepfakes require authentication; lawyers should challenge suspect evidence properly.

quiz.q: When might client informed consent be needed before using an AI tool?
opts: When confidential client information would be input into a tool with risks of disclosure or use beyond the matter, under applicable rules
quiz.x: Guidance such as ABA Opinion 512 recognises consent may be required depending on the tool's risks.

quiz.q: A lawyer bills a client for six hours spent learning how to use a general AI tool. Is this appropriate?
opts: Only if the client is a large company
Yes, since it benefits the client
Generally not — learning general tools is part of maintaining competence, not chargeable client work
quiz.x: Learning general technology is overhead for competence, not client work.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST reduces privilege risk when using AI?
opts: Using any tool but deleting chats afterwards
Using approved tools under strict confidentiality terms, limiting shared information and following firm policy
quiz.x: Confidentiality arrangements and minimisation reduce the risk of waiver arguments.

quiz.q: A legal aid organisation launches a public AI chatbot. Which design feature MOST protects users?
opts: Clear limitations, accuracy checks and easy escalation to human legal help
quiz.x: Vulnerable users need accuracy, transparency about limits and human help.

modules.d: A written protocol governing responsible AI use in your practice or legal department.
modules.body:
From individual use to practice-wide protocol

Your capstone is a practical AI protocol for your firm, chambers, legal department or compliance team. It should allow lawyers to use AI confidently for the right tasks while protecting clients, courts and the practice.

Protocol components

  1. Purpose and scope: which people, matters and tools the protocol covers.
  2. Principles: lawyer responsibility, confidentiality, verification, candour, fairness and client trust.
  3. Approved tools and uses: a list of approved tools with permitted uses (for example summarising client-provided documents, drafting from precedents, translation with review) and prohibited uses (for example relying on AI for authorities without verification, entering client data into unapproved tools).
  4. Data and confidentiality rules: classification of information, anonymisation requirements, client consent triggers, and client guideline compliance.
  5. Verification standard: every authority, quotation, pinpoint, statutory reference and factual assertion verified in authoritative sources before use; currency checks.
  6. Court and regulatory rules: compliance with practice directions on AI disclosure and certification.
  7. Supervision: review requirements by seniority and matter risk; training for juniors and staff.
  8. Billing: rules on time recording and fee arrangements involving AI.
  9. Incident response: what to do if an error is discovered or confidential data is exposed — including prompt correction with courts and notification obligations.
  10. Review: owner and review date.
Make verification visible. Many practices add a simple verification checklist to the file for any AI-assisted court filing or opinion: authorities retrieved and read; quotations checked; pinpoints confirmed; currency checked; facts traced to evidence; reviewer name and date. It takes minutes and could prevent sanctions.

Implementation

Approve the protocol through practice leadership; procure approved tools; train every lawyer and staff member, including practical exercises showing how AI fabricates authorities; integrate checklists into document management; and review after three months. Measure time saved, error and near-miss reports, client feedback and compliance.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit the protocol (no more than six pages plus checklists), one completed verification checklist for a sample AI-assisted document, and a one-page briefing for practice leadership. Your mentor reviews it for completeness, legal accuracy for your jurisdiction and practicality.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my legal AI protocol drafter. Using my practice type, jurisdictions and approved tools, draft a protocol with the ten components from this module in under six pages. Include a one-page verification checklist for AI-assisted filings and opinions, and an incident response procedure for errors and data exposure. Flag every rule I must confirm against my bar or law society and court practice directions.

📚 Glossary

  • AI protocol: practice-wide rules for responsible AI use
  • Verification checklist: record of checks performed on AI-assisted work
  • Incident response: steps taken when an error or data exposure is discovered
  • Near miss: an error caught before it caused harm

📖 References

  • American Bar Association — Formal Opinion 512 (2024).
  • Law Society of England and Wales — Generative AI guidance.
  • Court practice directions on AI — check each relevant court.

quiz.q: Which protocol component MOST directly prevents fabricated citations reaching a court?
quiz.x: Mandatory verification of authorities before use addresses fabrication.

quiz.q: A lawyer discovers after filing that an AI-assisted submission misquoted a statute. According to the incident response component, what should happen?
opts: Promptly correct the record with the court and record the incident
Ask the opponent not to mention it
quiz.x: Prompt correction and recording support candour and learning.

quiz.q: Which use should the protocol PROHIBIT?
opts: Relying on AI-generated authorities without verification
Drafting from approved precedents with review
Summarising client-provided documents in an approved tool
quiz.x: Unverified authorities create serious professional risk.

quiz.q: Why should training include exercises showing AI fabricating authorities?
opts: Because seeing fabrication in practice makes lawyers understand the need for verification
quiz.x: Experiential training builds lasting vigilance.

quiz.q: Which metric BEST indicates whether the protocol is working safely?
opts: Error and near-miss reports, compliance checks and time saved
quiz.x: Safety and benefit metrics together show effectiveness.

quiz.q: Where should client consent triggers be documented?
quiz.x: Consent relates to how client information is handled.

quiz.q: A court issues a new practice direction requiring certification of AI use. Which protocol component must be updated?
quiz.x: Court rules must be reflected and followed.

quiz.q: Who should be named as owner of the protocol?
opts: A responsible lawyer or committee who reviews and updates it
quiz.x: Ownership ensures review as tools and rules change.

quiz.q: A protocol is 30 pages long and rarely consulted. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Reduce the core to six pages with practical checklists embedded in workflows
quiz.x: Concise protocols with integrated checklists are used.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST captures the purpose of the protocol?
opts: To enable confident, responsible AI use while protecting clients, courts and the practice
quiz.x: Protocols enable safe use rather than prohibit it.
